c.tagline: West Africa's electric mega-city, pulsing on a lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; fares for yellow cabs and unmarked taxis are negotiated upfront, or set via ride-hailing apps.

emergency.note: 112 is Nigeria's toll-free unified emergency number (police, ambulance, fire); Lagos State Emergency Management Agency (LASEMA) can also be reached at 767.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Ikeja: Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Ikeja, Lagos

avoid.reason: Hide valuables; use caution on the mainland (Oshodi, Mushin, Ajegunle) and in traffic. Victoria Island/Ikoyi are more secure.

hood_desc: Lagos's glossy commercial core, packed with high-rise hotels, malls, embassies and rooftop bars; ideal for business travelers and anyone wanting nightlife within walking distance.
A leafy, upmarket residential enclave with tree-lined streets, art galleries and fine-dining restaurants; suits travelers seeking a quieter, refined base close to VI.
A sprawling, newer coastal district of gated estates, malls and beach clubs; popular with younger visitors, expats and beach lovers, though it's the furthest area from the airport.
The mainland hub around the international airport, with business hotels, GRA gardens and shopping malls; best for travelers prioritizing airport convenience or short layovers.
The historic heart of the city, home to colonial-era buildings, bustling markets like Balogun and the National Museum; suits culture seekers wanting old Lagos, though it's crowded and less polished.

water.note: Tap water is generally unsafe due to contamination risk; use bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Fares on BRT and the rail lines are paid with a reloadable Cowry Card tapped at turnstiles or readers, purchasable and topped up at stations. Danfo minibuses and keke napep tricycles are cash-only, paid directly to the driver or conductor in small naira notes.
transit.hours: BRT and rail generally run about 5:30am-10pm; danfo buses run informally from dawn until roughly 9-10pm. There is no reliable 24-hour public transit; ride-hailing apps (Uber/Bolt) are the safer option at night.
transit.note: Traffic ('go-slow') is severe and unpredictable; a 20-minute off-peak journey can take 2+ hours at rush hour.

transit.m: BRT bus via nearby Ikeja stops, transfer required (~90 min)

tip.r: Not traditionally expected but increasingly common in upscale restaurants and hotels (~10%); rounding up is standard for taxis and ride-hailing drivers.

food.name: Jollof Rice
food.desc: Smoky tomato-and-pepper rice cooked until the base catches, served with fried plantain and chicken or beef; the dish Lagos will argue about all night.

places.name: Terra Kulture
places.note: Arts centre restaurant that is the standard introduction to Nigerian classics for visitors.

places.name: Bungalow Restaurant & Lounge
places.note: Polished Nigerian and continental menu; reliable party-style jollof with sides.

places.name: Yakoyo
places.note: Long-running mainland buka-style spot doing generous plates at local prices.

food.name: Suya
food.desc: Thin beef skewers rubbed with yaji, a groundnut and chilli spice mix, grilled over wood coals and served with raw onion and tomato in newspaper.

places.name: Glover Court Suya
places.note: The most famous suya address in Lagos, grilling on the roadside for decades.

places.name: Obalende suya grills
places.note: Cluster of night-time mallam grills; go late, order by weight, expect real heat.

places.name: Suya Republic
places.note: Sit-down version with cleaner setting and beer, popular on the island.

food.name: Egusi Soup with Pounded Yam
food.desc: Melon-seed soup thickened with palm oil, bitterleaf and assorted meat, eaten by hand with smooth pounded yam swallow.

places.name: Terra Kulture
places.note: Consistently good egusi and pounded yam, with staff used to explaining the swallow.

places.name: Jevinik Restaurant
places.note: Known for eastern Nigerian soups and hearty assorted-meat bowls.

places.name: Yellow Chilli
places.note: Modernised Nigerian menu; a comfortable first stop for soups and swallows.

food.name: Amala with Ewedu and Gbegiri
food.desc: The Yoruba mainland staple: dark yam-flour swallow with slippery ewedu greens, bean gbegiri and peppery stew topped with offal or goat.

places.name: Amala Shitta
places.note: Legendary mainland canteen; queues at lunch, cash and confidence required.

places.name: Amala Skye
places.note: Popular Ikeja amala house with a wide spread of stews and proteins.

places.name: White House
places.note: Cheap, busy student-area buka with a big choice of swallows and soups.

food.name: Asun
food.desc: Smoked goat meat chopped small and tossed hot with scotch bonnet, onion and peppers; Lagos party food eaten with a cold drink.

places.name: Bature Brewery
places.note: Craft beer garden where peppered goat and grills are the standard order.

places.name: Obalende night grills
places.note: Same strip as the suya mallams; asun and peppered gizzard from open grills.

places.name: Bungalow Restaurant & Lounge
places.note: Cleaner sit-down version of asun on the small-chops side of the menu.

food.name: Puff-Puff
food.desc: Deep-fried sweet dough balls, crisp outside and airy inside, sold hot from roadside pans and stacked on every Lagos small-chops platter.

places.name: Yaba market fry stalls
places.note: Street pans frying puff-puff and akara through the afternoon; buy by the scoop.

places.name: Mama Cass
places.note: Nationwide Nigerian fast-food chain, dependable for small chops and pastries.

places.name: Balogun Market food row
places.note: Market vendors selling puff-puff, boli and roast corn to traders all day.

food.name: Chapman
food.desc: Lagos's own soft cocktail: Fanta and soda mixed with Angostura bitters, blackcurrant and citrus slices over ice; usually served alcohol-free.

places.name: Bungalow Restaurant & Lounge
places.note: Signature-style Chapman in a jug, the classic island version.

places.name: Terra Kulture
places.note: Easy pairing with a Nigerian lunch before a gallery or theatre visit.

places.name: RSVP
places.note: Smart cocktail bar that does a dressed-up Chapman alongside proper drinks.

food.name: Palm Wine
food.desc: Milky sap tapped from palm trees, sweet when fresh and increasingly sour and alcoholic as the day goes on; drunk from calabash or bottle.

places.name: Jevinik Restaurant
places.note: Serves palm wine alongside eastern soups, the traditional pairing.

places.name: Nkoyo
places.note: Pan-African menu with palm wine and other West African drinks by the jug.

places.name: Yakoyo
places.note: Mainland buka setting where palm wine is drunk cold with pepper soup.

landmarks: Lekki-Ikoyi Link Bridge
Nigeria's first cable-stayed bridge, its elegant curved silhouette lit up at night makes it Lagos's most Instagrammed modern landmark.
National Theatre
An iconic mid-century modernist building shaped like a giant military hat, standing as a cultural symbol of Nigeria since the 1970s.
Nike Art Gallery
A four-story gallery packed floor to ceiling with thousands of contemporary Nigerian artworks, one of West Africa's largest art collections.
Tafawa Balewa Square
A grand ceremonial ground marked by twin towers and a golden eagle monument, the site of Nigeria's independence celebrations.
Third Mainland Bridge
One of Africa's longest bridges, stretching across the Lagos Lagoon and offering dramatic sunrise and sunset photo opportunities.
Freedom Park
A former colonial prison transformed into a vibrant cultural park with an obelisk monument, live music, and open-air art installations.
Lekki Conservation Centre
Home to West Africa's longest canopy walkway, suspended high above a lush nature reserve teeming with monkeys and birdlife.
Eko Atlantic City
An ambitious land-reclamation megacity rising from the Atlantic coastline, showcasing Lagos's futuristic skyline ambitions.
Cathedral Church of Christ, Marina
A striking Gothic Revival Anglican cathedral in the heart of Lagos Island, blending colonial-era grandeur with historic significance.
Balogun Market
A sprawling, chaotic, and vibrant open-air market in the heart of Lagos Island, capturing the raw energy and color of West Africa's largest city.

train.note: NRC's Lagos-Ibadan standard-gauge service (via Abeokuta) is the main intercity train from Lagos; book at nrc.gov.ng or at the station. Urban Blue and Red Line rail also serve metropolitan Lagos. There are no international trains.

bus.note: ABC Transport runs cross-border coaches from Lagos (Jibowu/Amuwo Odofin) to Accra via Benin and Togo - carry your passport and ECOWAS travel documents and allow time for slow border crossings. Other operators such as GUO and Cross Country also serve the West-African corridor.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries. Government LAGFERRY and private operators run commuter boats across Lagos Lagoon (CMS, Ikorodu, Badagry and others) within the city only.

half.name: Cotonou
half.blurb: Benin's largest city, known for its bustling markets and lagoon-side location.

half.name: Porto-Novo
half.blurb: Benin's official capital, known for its blend of Afro-Brazilian and colonial architecture.

half.name: Ibadan
half.blurb: One of West Africa's largest cities, known for its university and vibrant markets.

half.name: Abeokuta
half.blurb: Yoruba city built among granite rock outcrops, known for its dyed textiles and rich heritage.

half.name: Lekki
half.blurb: Upscale peninsula district of Lagos known for beaches, modern development, and nightlife.

full.name: Lomé
full.blurb: Togo's coastal capital, known for bustling markets and breezy Atlantic beaches.

full.name: Benin City
full.blurb: Historic capital of the Edo people, famed for centuries-old bronze and ivory artistry.

full.name: Ilorin
full.blurb: Kwara State capital blending Yoruba and Fulani heritage with historic mosques.

full.name: Oyo
full.blurb: Historic Yoruba city in southwestern Nigeria known for its royal traditions.
